title: Demystifying evals for AI agents

key_points.claim: Research agent quality is context-relative and lacks binary unit-test signals; standards differ by task type.
key_points.evidence_quote: research quality can only be judged relative to the task. What counts as “comprehensive,” “well-sourced,” or even “correct” depends on context

key_points.claim: Research evals face specific challenges: expert disagreement, shifting ground truth, and open-ended outputs.
key_points.evidence_quote: experts may disagree on whether a synthesis is comprehensive, ground truth shifts as reference content changes constantly, and longer, more open-ended outputs create more room for mistakes.

key_points.claim: Recommended approach for research agents is combining grader types: groundedness, coverage, source quality, exact match where answers are objective, and LLM checks for synthesis.
key_points.evidence_quote: Groundedness checks verify that claims are supported by retrieved sources, coverage checks define key facts a good answer must include, and source quality checks confirm the consulted sources are authoritative

key_points.claim: LLM rubrics for research agents should be frequently calibrated against expert human judgment.
key_points.evidence_quote: LLM-based rubrics should be frequently calibrated against expert human judgment to grade these agents effectively.

key_points.claim: Use both pass@k and pass^k to handle non-determinism; choose by product need.
key_points.evidence_quote: pass@k for tools where one success matters, pass^k for agents where consistency is essential.

key_points.claim: Start small: 20-50 tasks drawn from real failures suffice initially.
key_points.evidence_quote: 20-50 simple tasks drawn from real failures is a great start.

key_points.claim: Tasks must be unambiguous with reference solutions; a 0% pass rate usually signals a broken task.
key_points.evidence_quote: A good task is one where two domain experts would independently reach the same pass/fail verdict.

key_points.claim: Build balanced problem sets testing both when a behavior should and shouldn't occur (e.g., search vs. answering from knowledge).
key_points.evidence_quote: Test both the cases where a behavior *should* occur and where it *shouldn't*. One-sided evals create one-sided optimization.

key_points.claim: Grade outcomes rather than exact paths, and give partial credit for multi-component tasks.
key_points.evidence_quote: it’s often better to grade what the agent produced, not the path it took.

key_points.claim: LLM-as-judge best practices: calibrate to humans, allow an 'Unknown' escape, grade each rubric dimension with an isolated judge.
key_points.evidence_quote: grade each dimension with an isolated LLM-as-judge rather than using one to grade all dimensions.

key_points.claim: Grader bugs can massively distort scores (CORE-Bench example).
key_points.evidence_quote: Opus 4.5 initially scored 42% on CORE-Bench... After fixing bugs and using a less constrained scaffold, Opus 4.5’s score jumped to 95%.

key_points.claim: Isolate trials in clean environments; shared state causes correlated failures or inflated results.
key_points.evidence_quote: Claude gaining an unfair advantage on some tasks by examining the git history from previous trials.

key_points.claim: Read transcripts to validate graders; don't trust scores at face value.
key_points.evidence_quote: we do not take eval scores at face value until someone digs into the details of the eval and reads some transcripts.

key_points.claim: Monitor for eval saturation; near-saturated evals hide capability gains.
key_points.evidence_quote: An eval at 100% tracks regressions but provides no signal for improvement.

key_points.claim: Evals should be complemented by production monitoring, A/B tests, user feedback, and human review; maintained as living artifacts with clear ownership.
key_points.evidence_quote: A complete picture includes production monitoring, user feedback, A/B testing, manual transcript review, and systematic human evaluation.

reliability_notes: Primary source from Anthropic engineering, based on internal experience and customer work. It is practitioner guidance rather than peer-reviewed. The research-agent section is short and mostly conceptual, with no quantitative results. Some anecdotes involve Anthropic's own models.
